desc:
There are n tasks numbered 0..n-1 and each must be done exactly once, one after another. Every rule [a, b] in rules says that task a must be done somewhere before task b.

Count the orders of all n tasks that obey every rule, modulo 1,000,000,007. Rules may repeat and may contradict each other (then the answer is 0).

n = 3, rules = [[0,1]]          ->  3
n = 3, rules = [[0,1],[1,2]]    ->  1
n = 3, rules = [[0,1],[1,0]]    ->  0
n = 4, rules = [[0,2],[1,2]]    ->  8
constraints: rules[i] = [a, b] with 0 ≤ a, b < n and a != b
hints: Trying all n! orders is too slow for n = 14 (about 87 billion). Notice that two partial orders that finished the same set of tasks have the same future.
State = the set of tasks already done, stored as a bitmask. A task may be done next only if all tasks that must come before it are in the set.

Let pred[v] be the bitmask of tasks that must precede v. Let dp[mask] be the number of valid orders of the tasks in mask. Then dp[mask | 1<<v] += dp[mask] whenever v is not in mask and pred[v] is a subset of mask.
editorial: The number of ways to finish does not depend on the order in which the tasks of a prefix were done, only on which tasks they are. So count valid prefixes by their set. dp[0] = 1. For every mask with dp[mask] > 0 and every task v not in the mask, if pred[v] & mask == pred[v] (all predecessors done), add dp[mask] to dp[mask | (1 << v)]. The answer is dp[(1 << n) - 1].

Contradictory rules (cycles) simply leave the full mask unreachable, giving 0. This counts the topological orderings of the rule graph. Time O(2<sup>n</sup> · n), memory O(2<sup>n</sup>). Plain backtracking over orders works for n up to about 9 but is far too slow for 14.
